# Attributes and Buckets

Three card keys that change what a [state map](./state-maps) reads: `ranges_attribute` and `state_attribute` read an attribute instead of the state, and `state_classification` decides which states count as active, inactive or a group of your own. They are top-level keys on the button, elbow and slider cards; `state_classification` works on the data grid and astrometrics cards too.

## `ranges_attribute`

**`ranges_attribute` makes the number keys (`zero`, `above:N`, `between:N:M` ...) compare an attribute instead of the state.** Use it for an entity whose state is not a number: a light is `on`, a cover `open`, but their brightness and position are numbers in attributes.

- `brightness_pct` is a light's brightness as `0` to `100` (Home Assistant stores it as `0` to `255`), so limits read as percentages. Any other value is an attribute name, such as `current_position` or `color_temp`.
- It applies to every state map on the card at once: colours, borders, text and icons. Exact state keys and `active` / `inactive` still read the state.
- When the light is off, `brightness_pct` is `0`, so `zero` and `below:N` keys match before `inactive` does. Use an `"off"` key for the off look, as below.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: light.tv
preset: lozenge
ranges_attribute: brightness_pct # range keys compare the brightness, 0 to 100
show_icon: true
text:
  name:
    show: true
tap_action:
  action: toggle
icon_style:
  color:
    active: match-light
    inactive: var(--lcards-gray)
  icon:
    "off": mdi:lightbulb-off
    above:90: mdi:lightbulb-alert # brighter than 90 %
    below:20: mdi:lightbulb-outline # dimmer than 20 %
    default: mdi:lightbulb
style:
  card:
    color:
      background:
        "off": var(--lcars-gray)
        above:70: var(--lcars-yellow)
        active: alpha(match-light, 0.5)
```

::: details More about ranges_attribute
- **A missing attribute,** or one that is not a number, leaves the range keys reading the state. For a light that state is `on`, so no range key matches.
- **The button's [`ranges`](/cards/button/components#ranges)** (preset switching) compare the same attribute; a `ranges` entry can name its own with `attribute`.
- **Parts with their own entity** read their own state: an elbow segment with `entity_id`, and data grid cells. MSD [line and shape overlays](/cards/msd/line-overlay#dynamic-styling) take their own `ranges_attribute`.
:::

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `ranges_attribute` | string | the state | The attribute the number keys compare. `brightness_pct`: a light's brightness, 0 to 100. `state`: the state, as when unset |

## `state_attribute`

**`state_attribute` makes the exact keys match an attribute's value instead of the state.** Use it when an attribute says more than the state: a thermostat's state is its mode (`heat`), but `hvac_action` says whether it is heating right now (`heating`, `idle`).

- The attribute is checked first; when no key matches its value, the state is checked as usual. `active`, `inactive` and `unavailable` always follow the state.
- It applies to every state map on the card: icon colour and icon, `icon_area_background`, background, border and text colours.
- It works alongside `ranges_attribute`: one attribute for the exact keys, another for the number keys.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: climate.living_room
preset: lozenge
state_attribute: hvac_action # heating, cooling, idle or off
show_icon: true
icon: mdi:thermostat
text:
  name:
    show: true
icon_style:
  color:
    heating: var(--lcars-alert-red)
    cooling: var(--lcards-blue)
    idle: var(--lcards-gray)
    "off": var(--lcards-gray)
icon_area_background:
  heating: alpha(var(--lcars-alert-red), 0.15)
  cooling: alpha(var(--lcards-blue), 0.15)
  idle: transparent
```

::: details More about state_attribute
- **Booleans and empty values:** the value is turned into text before it is matched, so a `true` / `false` attribute matches the keys `"true"` and `"false"` (quoted), and an empty (`null`) attribute matches `"null"`.
- **A missing attribute** is skipped, and the state is matched as usual.
- **Parts with their own entity** (an elbow segment with `entity_id`, data grid cells) match their own state. MSD [line and shape overlays](/cards/msd/line-overlay#dynamic-styling) take their own `state_attribute`.
:::

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `state_attribute` | string | - | The attribute whose value is matched against exact keys before the state, such as `hvac_action`, `effect` or `preset_mode` |

## `state_classification`

**`state_classification` decides which states count as `active` and `inactive`, and where every other state goes.** Use it when the built-in lists get it wrong for your entity, or to send unlisted states to `default`.

- States you list win over the built-in lists: `inactive: [home]` makes `home` inactive although it is normally active.
- `else` is the group for every state no list names. It is `inactive` unless you set it; `else: default` makes those states use your `default` colour instead of the preset's inactive colour.
- `unavailable` and `unknown` always count as `unavailable`. An exact state key in a colour map still wins over any group.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: input_select.lcards_test_mode
preset: lozenge
text:
  name:
    show: true
state_classification:
  active: [alpha] # alpha counts as active
  else: default # beta and gamma use default, not inactive
style:
  card:
    color:
      background:
        active: var(--lcars-green)
        default: var(--lcars-blue)
```

::: details More about state_classification
- **The order states are sorted in:** `unavailable` and `unknown`, then your `active` list, your `inactive` list, your own groups, the built-in active list, and last `else`.
- **`else: active`** treats every state as active except `unavailable` and `unknown`, which suits an entity that is only ever on or unavailable.
- **In the card editor,** `else` is a dropdown; the lists are set in YAML.
- **Data grid and astrometrics cards** use the card's `state_classification` for every cell's or point's entity.
:::

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `state_classification.active` | list | - | More states that count as active, added to the built-in list |
| `state_classification.inactive` | list | - | States that count as inactive, even ones on the built-in active list |
| `state_classification.<name>` | list | - | The states in a group of your own: see [Custom buckets](#custom-buckets) |
| `state_classification.else` | string | `inactive` | The group for every other state: `active`, `inactive`, `default` or one of your own names |

### Custom buckets

**Any other key in `state_classification` makes a group of your own, which you then use as a key in state maps.** Use it to give several states one colour, such as every zone that means "at work".

- A group's name can be anything except `active`, `inactive`, `unavailable`, `default`, `else` and `unknown`.
- `else` can name one of your groups, so every unlisted state lands in it.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: input_select.lcards_test_mode
preset: lozenge
text:
  name:
    show: true
state_classification:
  ready: [alpha]
  standby: [beta]
  else: alert # gamma and anything else
style:
  card:
    color:
      background:
        ready: var(--lcars-green)
        standby: var(--lcars-blue)
        alert: var(--lcars-alert-red)
        unavailable: var(--lcars-gray)
```

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `state_classification.<name>` | list | - | The states in the group `<name>`; use `<name>:` as a key in any state map on the card |

---

<!-- https://lcards.unimatrix01.ca/dev/core/colours/state-maps.html -->

# State Maps

**A state map is a colour key given one colour per state instead of one colour.** The card picks the colour that matches its entity's state, and changes it as the state changes. Each value is any [colour value](../colours#colour-value-formats).

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: climate.living_room
preset: lozenge
text:
  name:
    show: true
style:
  card:
    color:
      background:
        heat: var(--lcars-alert-red) # an exact state
        cool: var(--lcards-blue)
        active: var(--lcars-orange) # any other "on" state
        default: var(--lcars-gray)
```

## State keys

**State keys pick a colour by what the entity is doing: an exact state, or on, off and unavailable.** Use `active` and `inactive` for anything that switches; add an exact state (`heat`, `playing`) where one state needs its own colour.

- An exact state key wins over `active` and `inactive`, so `heat:` colours a heating thermostat even though `heat` also counts as active.
- On a button or elbow, a preset or the theme fills in the background and text colour for the current state group when your map does not name it. With only `default` set, an off entity shows the preset's (or theme's) inactive colour, not your `default`; set `inactive` too, or use [`state_classification`](./attributes#state-classification) `else: default`.
- `hover` and `pressed` colour a [button's](/cards/button/styles#style-card) background and border while the pointer is over it or it is pressed.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: climate.living_room
preset: lozenge
text:
  label:
    show: true
    content: Climate
    position: top-left
    color:
      default: var(--lcards-moonlight)
      active: var(--lcards-orange)
      unavailable: var(--lcars-alert-red)
  state:
    show: true
    content: "{entity.state}"
    position: center
    color:
      heat: var(--lcars-alert-red)
      cool: var(--lcards-blue)
      auto: var(--lcards-orange)
      default: var(--lcards-moonlight)
style:
  card:
    color:
      background:
        default: var(--ha-card-background)
        active: alpha(var(--lcards-orange), 0.08)
  border:
    color:
      default: var(--lcards-gray)
      active: var(--lcards-orange)
      heat: var(--lcars-alert-red)
      cool: var(--lcards-blue)
      unavailable: var(--lcars-alert-red)
    width: 2
```

::: details More about active and inactive
- **`active`** is any of these states: `on` · `open` · `playing` · `home` · `heat` · `cool` · `auto` · `fan_only` · `dry` · `locked` · `armed_home` · `armed_away` · `armed_night` · `armed_vacation` · `armed_custom_bypass` · `cleaning` · `mowing` · `docked` · `returning` · `paused` · `active` · `above_horizon`.
- **`inactive`** is every other state, such as `off`, `closed`, `idle`, `standby`, `unlocked` or `disarmed`, except `unavailable` and `unknown`.
- **Your own groups:** [`state_classification`](./attributes#state-classification) adds states to these lists, and makes groups of your own.
- **Quote `"on"` and `"off"`** when you use them as exact keys: Home Assistant's code editor reads them as true and false otherwise.
:::

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `default` | colour | - | Any state no other key matches, and a card with no entity |
| `active` | colour | - | The entity is on, open, playing, heating ...: see the list above |
| `inactive` | colour | - | Any other state |
| `unavailable` | colour | - | The state is `unavailable` or `unknown` |
| `hover` | colour | - | Button background and border while the pointer is over the card |
| `pressed` | colour | - | Button background and border while it is pressed |
| `<state>` | colour | - | Exactly this state, such as `heat`, `cooling`, `buffering` |

## Number keys

**Number keys pick a colour by the entity's value: zero, above or below a limit, or inside a band.** Use them for a sensor, a battery or a level, so the colour turns yellow or red past a limit.

- The value is the state read as a number. For an entity whose state is not a number (a light is `on`), [`ranges_attribute`](./attributes#ranges-attribute) compares an attribute instead.
- When several range keys match, the most specific wins: a `between` beats an `above`, which beats a `below`. Among `between` keys the narrowest band wins, among `above` keys the highest limit, and among `below` keys the lowest.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: input_number.lcards_test_power
preset: lozenge
text:
  name:
    show: true
style:
  card:
    color:
      background:
        zero: var(--lcars-alert-red) # exactly 0
        below:20: var(--lcars-alert-red) # critical
        below:50: var(--lcars-alert-yellow) # low
        between:40:60: var(--lcars-blue) # wins over below:50 from 40 to 49
        non_zero: var(--lcars-green) # any other level
        default: var(--lcars-gray)
```

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `zero` | colour | - | The value is exactly `0`. Checked before the range keys |
| `non_zero` | colour | - | Any other number, when no range key matched |
| `above:N` | colour | - | The value is more than `N`: `above:50` |
| `at_least:N` | colour | - | The value is `N` or more: `at_least:50` |
| `below:N` | colour | - | The value is less than `N`: `below:20` |
| `at_most:N` | colour | - | The value is `N` or less: `at_most:20` |
| `between:N:M` | colour | - | From `N` to `M`, both included: `between:20:80` |
| `between_exclusive:N:M` | colour | - | Between `N` and `M`, neither included: `between_exclusive:20:80` |

## Resolution order

**The card checks the keys in this order and uses the first that matches.**

1. **The [`state_attribute`](./attributes#state-attribute) value**, when the card sets it: a key equal to that attribute's value.
2. **The exact state:** a key equal to the state, such as `heat`.
3. **`zero`:** the value is `0`.
4. **The range keys** (`above`, `at_least`, `below`, `at_most`, `between`, `between_exclusive`): the most specific match, as in [Number keys](#number-keys).
5. **`non_zero`:** any other number.
6. **The state group:** `active`, `inactive`, `unavailable`, or a group of your own from [`state_classification`](./attributes#state-classification).
7. **`default`.**

Steps 3 to 5 read the state as a number, or the attribute named by [`ranges_attribute`](./attributes#ranges-attribute). Icons chosen by state (`icon_style.icon`) follow the same order.

## Where colour maps are valid

**State maps work in most colour keys that belong to the card's entity.** On these pages the key tables say "state map" where one works.

- **Button and elbow:** `style.card.color.background`, `style.border.color`, `style.text.default.color`, `text.<field>.color`, `style.text.<field>.color` and `style.text.<field>.background`, `icon_style.color`, `icon_area_background`, and `shape_texture.config.color` (`color_a`, `color_b`, `edge_glow_color`).
- **Elbow:** `elbow.segment.color`, each segment's `color` in `elbow.segments`, `symbiont.imprint.background` and `symbiont.imprint.text.color`.
- **Slider:** `style.gauge.indicator.color` and `.border.color`, `style.gauge.progress_bar.color`, `style.ranges[].color`, `style.shaped.fill.color`, `style.border.<side>.color` and more: see the [Slider Card](/cards/slider-card/styles) pages.
- **Other cards:** data grid cell `color` and `background` ([Conditional colours](/cards/data-grid/data#conditional-colours)), MSD line and shape `style.color` ([Dynamic styling](/cards/msd/line-overlay#dynamic-styling)), and astrometrics points and objects ([Colours from entities](/cards/astrometrics/data#colours-from-entities)).

The settings of a [background animation](/core/effects/background-animations) and a button's `divider.color` take one colour (or, for a background animation, a template), not a state map.

## Template strings as colour values

**A colour key can be a template, which works the colour out each time the entities it reads change.** Use it when a state map cannot say it: two entities at once, or a rule with `and` and `or`.

- Jinja2 (`{{ }}`, `{% %}`) and JavaScript (`[[[ ]]]`) templates work, as the whole value or as one value in a state map. The template must give a colour value.
- A Jinja2 template follows every entity it names. A JavaScript template that reads other entities needs them in `triggers_update` on the card: see [Templates](/core/templates/#manual-tracking-with-triggers-update).
- For most cases a state map with [`state_attribute`](./attributes#state-attribute) is simpler to read.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: climate.living_room
preset: lozenge
show_icon: true
icon: mdi:thermostat
text:
  name:
    show: true
icon_style:
  # red while heating, blue otherwise
  color: "{{ 'var(--lcars-alert-red)' if state_attr('climate.living_room', 'hvac_action') == 'heating' else 'var(--lcards-blue)' }}"
```

### Colour from another entity

**A state map follows the card's own entity; for a colour that follows a different entity, use a template.** A template can read any entity, whatever the card is bound to.

- Some parts have an entity of their own, and their state maps follow it: an elbow segment's `entity_id`, a data grid cell, an MSD line or shape's `entity`, and the `entity` in an astrometrics colour map.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-slider
entity: input_number.lcards_test_value # the slider sets this
preset: gauge-basic
style:
  gauge:
    indicator:
      # green while the toggle is on
      color: "{{ 'var(--lcards-green)' if is_state('input_boolean.lcards_test_toggle', 'on') else 'var(--lcards-gray)' }}"
```

---

<!-- https://lcards.unimatrix01.ca/dev/core/colours/values.html -->

# Colour Values

The colour values you write most: palette variables, theme tokens, colour functions that derive one colour from another, and `match-light`. The full list of accepted formats (hex, `rgb()`, `oklch()` ...) is on the [Colours](../colours#colour-value-formats) page.

## CSS variables

**`var(--name)` uses a colour variable, so the card follows the theme and the alert mode.** It is the usual way to colour a card.

- LCARdS sets the `--lcards-*` palette itself, so those variables are there with any Home Assistant theme. The `--lcars-*` variables come from the HA-LCARS theme.
- In an alert mode, LCARdS shifts both palettes, and every colour that uses them follows at once. Use [`base()`](#base) for a colour that should not change.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: lozenge
text:
  label:
    show: true
    content: PALETTE
    color: var(--lcards-moonlight)
style:
  card:
    color:
      background: var(--lcards-orange)
  border:
    color: var(--lcars-alert-red)
    width: 2
```

Some common ones:

| Variable | Notes |
|----------|-------|
| `var(--lcards-orange)`, `var(--lcards-orange-medium)` | LCARdS orange |
| `var(--lcards-blue)`, `var(--lcards-blue-light)` | LCARdS blue |
| `var(--lcards-moonlight)` | Near-white, for text and labels |
| `var(--lcards-gray)` | A standby grey |
| `var(--lcars-alert-red)`, `var(--lcars-alert-yellow)` | The HA-LCARS alert colours |

The [LCARdS CSS colour palette](../themes/#lcards-css-colour-palette) lists every `--lcards-*` shade.

## Theme token paths

**`theme:` followed by a token path takes a colour from the active theme.** Use it for colours that should match the theme's roles (primary, secondary, alert) rather than a fixed shade.

- A token path names a colour by its role, so changing the theme changes every card that uses it.
- Inside a colour function, a token path works without the `theme:` prefix: `alpha(colors.ui.primary, 0.4)`.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: lozenge
text:
  label:
    show: true
    content: THEME
    color: theme:colors.text.onDark
style:
  card:
    color:
      background: theme:colors.ui.secondary
  border:
    color: theme:colors.alert.red
    width: 2
```

Some common ones:

| Token | Notes |
|-------|-------|
| `theme:colors.ui.primary` | The theme's main structure colour |
| `theme:colors.ui.secondary` | The secondary structure colour |
| `theme:colors.text.onDark` | Text on a dark background |
| `theme:colors.alert.red` | The alert red |

[Themes](../themes/) lists the token paths.

## Computed colour tokens

**Colour functions derive a colour from another: a darker shade, a lighter one, a see-through one, or a mix of two.** Use them to make a hover colour, a dimmed background or a glow from one palette colour.

- The first argument is any colour value, including another function: functions nest. Amounts are `0` to `1`, or a percentage (`15%`).
- A function over a CSS variable stays live, so it follows the alert mode too.
- An argument can be a token path, with or without `theme:`. A `theme:` in front of the whole function changes nothing: `theme:alpha(colors.ui.primary, 0.4)` is `alpha(colors.ui.primary, 0.4)`.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: lozenge
text:
  label:
    show: true
    content: COMPUTED
    color: lighten(var(--lcards-blue), 30%)
style:
  card:
    color:
      background: alpha(darken(var(--lcards-orange), 0.2), 0.5)
  border:
    color: theme:alpha(colors.ui.primary, 0.4)
    width: 2
```

::: details More about colour functions
- **Leaving out the amount:** `darken()`, `lighten()`, `saturate()` and `desaturate()` use `0.2`, `alpha()` uses `1`, and `mix()` uses `0.5`.
- **`saturate()` and `desaturate()`** read a CSS variable's value at the moment the card draws, so after an alert-mode change they keep the old colour until the card draws again. The other functions follow at once.
:::

| Function | Example | Result |
|----------|---------|--------|
| `darken(colour, amount)` | `darken(var(--lcards-orange), 0.2)` | 20% towards black |
| `lighten(colour, amount)` | `lighten(var(--lcards-blue), 15%)` | 15% towards white |
| `alpha(colour, opacity)` | `alpha(var(--lcards-orange), 0.6)` | Opacity set to 60% |
| `saturate(colour, amount)` | `saturate(var(--lcards-orange-medium), 0.2)` | More vivid |
| `desaturate(colour, amount)` | `desaturate(var(--lcards-orange), 0.5)` | Closer to grey |
| `mix(colour1, colour2, weight)` | `mix(var(--lcars-red), var(--lcars-blue), 0.25)` | 25% of the first colour; the same as `color-mix(in srgb, var(--lcars-red) 25%, var(--lcars-blue))` |
| `base(colour)` | `base(var(--lcards-blue))` | The colour without the alert mode: see [base()](#base) |

### `base()`

**`base()` gives a variable's or token's normal (green alert) colour, whatever the alert mode.** Use it for a colour that must not change in red alert, such as a status light that means something on its own.

- `base()` takes a token path (`colors.ui.primary`), a variable (`var(--lcards-blue)`) or just its name (`--lcards-blue`).
- It works in every colour key, including animation and effect settings. A plain `var()` there follows the alert mode; wrap it in `base()` to keep it still.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: lozenge
text:
  label:
    show: true
    content: ALWAYS BLUE
style:
  card:
    color:
      # stays this blue in red alert
      background: base(--lcards-blue-lightest)
  border:
    color: alpha(base(colors.ui.primary), 0.5)
    width: 2
```

::: details More about base()
- **Where the normal colour comes from:** for `--lcars-*` variables, the values LCARdS records when the theme loads; for `--lcards-*` variables, the LCARdS green alert palette.
- **Other variables**, and a `--lcars-*` variable before the theme has loaded, give their current value, as `var()` would.
:::

## `match-light`

**`match-light` is the current colour of the card's light.** Use it to tint a button or slider the colour the light is set to.

- It works when the card's `entity` is a `light.` entity that is on. When the light is off there is no colour, so put `match-light` under `active` in a [state map](./state-maps) and give `inactive` its own colour.
- `match-brightness` is the light's brightness as an opacity from `0` to `1`, for use inside a colour function: `alpha(match-light, match-brightness)`.
- A white-only light gives a warm white, brighter as the light is brighter.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: light.tv
preset: lozenge
text:
  name:
    show: true
tap_action:
  action: toggle
style:
  card:
    color:
      background:
        active: alpha(match-light, match-brightness)
        inactive: var(--lcars-gray)
  border:
    color:
      active: match-light
      inactive: var(--lcars-gray)
    width: 2
```

<!-- https://lcards.unimatrix01.ca/dev/core/colours.html -->

# Colours

**Every colour key on every LCARdS card takes the same colour values: a CSS variable, a theme token, a colour function, or any CSS colour.** A colour key can also take a state map, which picks a colour from the card's entity state.

- Colours built from CSS variables and theme tokens follow the [alert mode](./alert-mode): when red alert shifts the palette, they change with it, without a refresh. Hex and named colours stay as they are.
- A state map (`active`, `inactive`, `above:50`, a state name ...) picks the colour as the entity changes; templates work too.

| Page | Covers |
|------|--------|
| [Colour Values](./colours/values) | CSS variables, theme tokens, colour functions such as `alpha()` and `darken()`, `base()`, `match-light` |
| [State Maps](./colours/state-maps) | Colours by state: state and number keys, the order they are checked in, where maps work, templates |
| [Attributes and Buckets](./colours/attributes) | Colours from an attribute (`ranges_attribute`, `state_attribute`) and your own state groups (`state_classification`) |

---

## Quick start

**Two examples to start from: one fixed colour, and a colour that follows the entity.**

- A fixed colour is a plain value. A colour that follows the entity is a map of states to colours, with `default` for everything else.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: lozenge
text:
  label:
    show: true
    content: FIXED
style:
  card:
    color:
      background: alpha(var(--lcars-blue), 0.6)
```

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: input_boolean.lcards_test_toggle
preset: lozenge
text:
  name:
    show: true
tap_action:
  action: toggle
style:
  card:
    color:
      background:
        active: var(--lcars-orange)
        inactive: var(--lcars-gray)
        unavailable: var(--lcars-alert-red)
```

## Colour value formats

**What you can write in a colour key.** Every format works in every colour key, on its own or as a value in a [state map](./colours/state-maps).

- Quote hex colours in YAML: unquoted, `#ff9900` starts a comment and the key is left empty.

| Format | Example | Notes |
|--------|---------|-------|
| CSS variable | `var(--lcards-orange)` | Any `--lcards-*`, `--lcars-*` or Home Assistant variable. See [CSS variables](./colours/values#css-variables) |
| Theme token path | `theme:colors.ui.primary` | A colour from the active theme. See [Theme token paths](./colours/values#theme-token-paths) |
| Colour function | `darken(var(--lcards-orange), 0.2)` | `alpha()`, `darken()`, `lighten()`, `saturate()`, `desaturate()`, `mix()`, `base()`. See [Computed colour tokens](./colours/values#computed-colour-tokens) |
| Hex | `"#F90"`, `"#FF9900"`, `"#FF990080"` | 3, 4, 6 or 8 digits; the last digit (of 4) or pair (of 8) is the alpha |
| Named colour | `black`, `orange`, `transparent` | Any CSS colour name, in lower case, and `currentColor` |
| RGB / HSL | `rgba(255, 153, 0, 0.5)`, `hsl(36 100% 50%)` | Comma or space syntax, optional `/ alpha` |
| Other CSS colours | `oklch(0.75 0.17 60)`, `color-mix(in srgb, red 25%, blue)` | `hwb()`, `lab()`, `lch()`, `oklab()`, `oklch()`, `color()`, `color-mix()` |
| Match light | `match-light` | The colour of the card's light entity. See [match-light](./colours/values#match-light) |

## Card keys

**Three top-level card keys change how state maps read the entity.** They are on the [Attributes and Buckets](./colours/attributes) page.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
entity: light.tv
preset: lozenge
ranges_attribute: brightness_pct # ranges compare the brightness, 0 to 100
text:
  name:
    show: true
style:
  card:
    color:
      background:
        above:70: var(--lcars-yellow)
        active: var(--lcars-orange)
        inactive: var(--lcars-gray)
```

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `ranges_attribute` | string | the state | The attribute that range keys (`above:N`, `between:N:M` ...) compare: see [ranges_attribute](./colours/attributes#ranges-attribute) |
| `state_attribute` | string | - | The attribute whose value picks exact-match keys: see [state_attribute](./colours/attributes#state-attribute) |
| `state_classification` | object | - | Which states count as active or inactive, and your own named groups: see [state_classification](./colours/attributes#state-classification) |

<!-- https://lcards.unimatrix01.ca/dev/core/datasources/ -->

# Data Sources

**A data source follows one entity in your browser, keeps its recent values, and runs them through processors that smooth, convert or otherwise work on them.** Cards show the results in [templates](../templates/#data-source-templates) as `{ds:name}` and plot them as [chart series](#data-sources-in-charts).

- Declare data sources under `data_sources` on any LCARdS card. Each key is a name you choose, and the name is how templates and charts find it.
- Names are shared by the whole dashboard: the first card to create a name sets it up, and a later card using the same name gets that data source, settings and all. Give each data source its own name.
- Data sources are created when the dashboard loads, preload some history, then follow live changes. They keep a limited number of recent points (see [`window_seconds`](#top-level-fields)), so for long spans of plain history, plot the entity on a [chart](../../cards/chart/series#where-the-data-comes-from) instead.

::: tip Try it
A card editor's **Main Engineering > Data Sources** tab creates and edits data sources without YAML, with a preview of each processor ([In the card editor](#in-the-card-editor)). The [Processor Reference](./processor-reference) has a live lab for every processor.
:::

## How a Data Source Works

**Each change of the entity goes into a rolling buffer of recent values, then through the processing pipeline, and each processor keeps its own result.** Templates and charts read the raw value or any processor's result.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    E[Entity updates] --> S[Subscribe]
    S --> H[Rolling history buffer]
    H --> P[Processing pipeline]
    P --> B1[Processor: smooth]
    B1 --> B2[Processor: scale]
    B2 --> OUT[Template / Chart]
```

## Basic Usage

**Name a data source under `data_sources`, give it an `entity`, and read it in a template with `{ds:name}`.** Without a format the value shows as Home Assistant shows numbers, with the entity's unit; with one, such as `:.1f`, you write your own unit.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: lozenge
data_sources:
  room_temp:
    entity: sensor.demo_temperature
    history:
      hours: 6
text:
  default:
    color: var(--lcars-black)
  native:
    content: "{ds:room_temp}" # Home Assistant's number format, with the unit
    position: top-left
  precise:
    content: "{ds:room_temp:.1f} °C" # your precision, your unit
    position: bottom-left
grid_options:
  rows: 2
```

## Configuration Options

**A data source needs only an `entity`; the other keys set how much it keeps, how often it updates cards, and how much history it preloads.** The defaults suit most cards.

- History is preloaded when the card loads: every recorded change over `history.hours`, or Home Assistant's hourly statistics when the recorder has none (for the entity state, not an attribute).
- The buffer holds a number of points, not a span of time: a sensor that reports once a minute keeps ten hours of values in the default 600 points, and a preload longer than that keeps only its newest points.
- A change after a quiet spell reaches cards at once. Rapid changes are merged before cards hear of them: at most one update every `min_emit_ms`, sent `coalesce_ms` after the last change of a burst, and never held back longer than `max_delay_ms`. The merged update carries the newest value; the buffer and the processors still see every change.

### Top-Level Fields

**Every key a data source takes, besides its processors.** Processors are under [Processors](#processors).

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: lozenge
data_sources:
  house_power:
    entity: sensor.demo_power # required: the entity to follow
    window_seconds: 120 # keep about 1,200 points
    min_emit_ms: 500 # update cards at most twice a second
    history:
      hours: 24
    processing:
      # each processor keeps its result under its own name
      kilowatts:
        type: scale
        input_range: [0, 1000]
        output_range: [0, 1]
      smoothed:
        type: smooth
        input_source: kilowatts # works on the kilowatts result
        method: exponential
        alpha: 0.3
text:
  default:
    color: var(--lcars-black)
  power:
    content: "{ds:house_power.smoothed:.2f} kW"
    position: top-left
grid_options:
  rows: 2
```

::: details More about the fields
- **Older names:** older configs may use camelCase (`windowSeconds`, `minEmitMs`, `coalesceMs`, `maxDelayMs`, `emitOnSameValue`) and `history.preload` for `history.enabled`. They still work, and the editor marks them as old names. If both spellings are set, the snake_case one wins.
- **States that are not numbers:** the states `on`, `true`, `active` and `open` count as 1, and `off`, `false`, `inactive` and `closed` as 0. Other words need `enum_mapping`; without it they are skipped, as are `unavailable` and `unknown`.
- **Home Assistant's code editor:** it reads unquoted `on`, `off`, `yes` and `no` as true or false, so quote them as `enum_mapping` keys: `"off": 0`.
:::

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `entity` | string | required | The entity to follow |
| `attribute` | string | the state | An attribute to follow instead of the state. `state` means the state |
| `enum_mapping` | object | - | Numbers for states that are not numbers, such as `heat: 2` and `cool: 1` |
| `window_seconds` | number / string | `60` | How many points the buffer keeps: about 10 per second of window, at least 60 and at most 1,000 (`60` keeps 600). Also takes a duration such as `"5m"` |
| `min_emit_ms` | number | `100` | The least time between updates sent to cards, ms (at least 10) |
| `coalesce_ms` | number | 40% of `min_emit_ms`, at least `20` | How long to wait after the last of several rapid changes before sending the merged update, ms (at least 20) |
| `max_delay_ms` | number | 3 x `coalesce_ms` | The longest an update may be held back while gathering, ms (at least `min_emit_ms`) |
| `emit_on_same_value` | boolean | `true` | Send an update even when the value didn't change |
| `history.enabled` | boolean | `true` | Preload history when the card loads |
| `history.hours` | number | `6` | Hours of history to preload, 1 to 168 |
| `history.days` | number | - | Days of history to preload, 1 to 7, instead of `hours`. `hours` wins when both are set |
| `processing` | object | - | Named processors: see [Processors](#processors) |

## Processors

**A processor works on the data source's values and keeps its result under its own name; `input_source` chains it after another processor.** Without `input_source` a processor reads the raw value.

- Read a processor's result in a template with `{ds:name.processor}`, and plot it with a chart series' `buffer`.
- A processor's result has no unit: give it a format and your own unit, such as `{ds:temp.fahrenheit:.0f} °F`.
- The [Processor Reference](./processor-reference) covers every option, with a live lab for each processor.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: lozenge
data_sources:
  room_temp_f:
    entity: sensor.demo_temperature
    processing:
      # Celsius to Fahrenheit
      fahrenheit:
        type: convert_unit
        from: c
        to: f
      # then smooth the converted value
      smooth_f:
        type: smooth
        input_source: fahrenheit
        method: exponential
        alpha: 0.2
text:
  default:
    color: var(--lcars-black)
  raw:
    content: "{ds:room_temp_f:.1f} °C"
    position: top-left
  converted:
    content: "{ds:room_temp_f.smooth_f:.1f} °F"
    position: bottom-left
grid_options:
  rows: 2
```

| Processor | Purpose | Main settings |
|-----------|---------|---------------|
| `convert_unit` | Convert between units | `from`, `to` (such as `c` and `f`) |
| `scale` | Map from one range to another | `input_range`, `output_range`, `curve` |
| `smooth` | Smooth noisy values | `method` (`exponential`, `moving_average`, `gaussian`), `alpha`, `window` |
| `round` | Round to decimal places | `precision`, `method` |
| `expression` | A JavaScript expression of your own | `expression` (uses `value`, `sources`, `Math`), `sources` |
| `clamp` | Keep within a minimum and maximum | `min`, `max` |
| `rate` | Rate of change per unit of time | `unit` (`per_second`, `per_minute`, `per_hour`), `smoothing` |
| `trend` | Increasing, decreasing or stable | `samples`, `threshold` |
| `delta` | Difference from the previous value | `absolute` |
| `duration` | Time spent meeting a condition | `condition`, `reset_on` |
| `statistics` | Min, max, mean and more over a window | `window`, `stats` |
| `threshold` | Two outputs either side of a threshold | `threshold`, `above`, `below`, `hysteresis` |

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `type` | string | required | The processor, from the list above |
| `input_source` | string | the raw value | The name of another processor in this data source whose result this one works on |
| `enabled` | boolean | `true` | `false` passes values through unchanged |

### In the card editor

**A card editor's Data Sources tab (under Main Engineering) creates and edits data sources without YAML.** In the data source dialog, the **Processing** tab shows:

- **A preview**: the processors run over the entity's own recent history (the span set under Timing & History, the way the data source preloads it), charted against the raw values. It updates as you edit; the selected processor's line is drawn heavier.
- **The pipeline**: each processor under its input, numbered in the order they run. Errors such as a missing input or a loop show above it.
- **The selected processor's settings**, edited in place: its name (renaming updates the processors that use it), its input (the raw value or another processor), and the type's options. **Edit as YAML** switches to its YAML.

The preview runs the same processor code as the dashboard. Live-only behaviour, such as a duration ticking between state changes, isn't shown.

## Accessing Values in Templates

**`{ds:name}` (or `{datasource:name}`) shows a data source's value in any text that takes [templates](../templates/#where-templates-work).** The rule: no format, and Home Assistant formats it with the unit; with a format, you control the output. The [Templates](../templates/#data-source-templates) page lists every format.

```yaml alternatives
# No format: Home Assistant's number format, with the entity's unit
"{ds:temp}"                            # → "21.4 °C"

# With a format: the number only, no unit
"{ds:temp:.1f}"                        # → "21.4"
"{ds:temp:.0f}"                        # → "21"
"{ds:temp:.1f} °C"                     # → "21.4 °C" (your own unit)

# A processor's result: a dot and its name, with either prefix
"{ds:temp.fahrenheit:.0f} °F"          # → "71 °F"
"{datasource:temp.fahrenheit:.0f} °F"  # the same
```

::: details More about values in templates
- **Data sources from other cards:** a card updates when the data sources in its own `data_sources` change. To show one another card defines, declare it in this card's `data_sources` too, with the same name.
- **One statistic:** a `statistics` processor holds several values; pick one with another dot. For a processor named `stats`: `{ds:temp.stats.max:.1f}`.
:::

## Data Sources in Charts

**A chart series can plot a data source's values, or one of its processors' results with `buffer`.** See the [Chart card](../../cards/chart/series#data-sources) for the series keys.

```yaml live
type: custom:lcards-chart
chart_type: line
data_sources:
  chart_temp:
    entity: sensor.demo_temperature
    processing:
      smoothed:
        type: smooth
        method: exponential
        alpha: 0.3
sources:
  - datasource: chart_temp
    name: Raw
  - datasource: chart_temp
    buffer: smoothed
    name: Smoothed
```

<!-- https://lcards.unimatrix01.ca/dev/core/datasources/processor-reference.html -->

# Processor Reference

Complete reference for all 12 DataSource processor types.

## Overview

Processors transform data as it flows through a DataSource. Each processor:
- Has a unique **name** (the key in the `processing` object)
- Specifies a **type** (one of 12 processor types)
- Optionally uses `input_source` to depend on another processor
- Outputs a value accessible in templates as `{datasource.processor_name}`

Each section has a **Try it** lab: it runs the real LCARdS processors over a day of generated sample history and charts the raw values against each processor's output. Select **Edit** to change the YAML; any `sensor.*` entity id gets a sample signal.

## Quick Reference

| Type | Purpose | Common Use |
|------|---------|------------|
| [`convert_unit`](#convert-unit) | Unit conversion | Temperature °F↔°C, power W↔kW |
| [`scale`](#scale) | Map range to range | 0-100 → 0-255, normalize values |
| [`smooth`](#smooth) | Reduce noise | Smooth jittery sensors |
| [`expression`](#expression) | Custom formula | Calculate derived values |
| [`statistics`](#statistics) | Min/max/mean/etc | Aggregate over time window |
| [`rate`](#rate) | Rate of change | Watts → watts/hour |
| [`trend`](#trend) | Direction detection | Increasing/decreasing/stable |
| [`duration`](#duration) | Time tracking | Time spent above threshold |
| [`threshold`](#threshold) | Binary conversion | Above/below → 1/0 |
| [`clamp`](#clamp) | Limit to range | Keep within min/max |
| [`round`](#round) | Round precision | 2 decimals, floor, ceil |
| [`delta`](#delta) | Change detection | Difference from last value |

---

## `convert_unit`

Convert between measurement units.

### Configuration

```yaml
processor_name:
  type: convert_unit
  from: c          # Source unit
  to: f            # Target unit
```

### Supported Units

**Temperature:**
- `c` (Celsius), `f` (Fahrenheit), `k` (Kelvin)

**Power:**
- `w`, `kw`, `mw`, `gw` (watts → gigawatts)

**Energy:**
- `wh`, `kwh`, `mwh` (watt-hours)
- `j`, `kj`, `mj` (joules)

**Distance:**
- `mm`, `cm`, `m`, `km` (metric)
- `in`, `ft`, `yd`, `mi` (imperial)

**Speed:**
- `ms` (meters/second), `kmh`, `mph`

**Pressure:**
- `hpa`, `bar`, `psi`, `mmhg`

**Data:**
- `b`, `kb`, `mb`, `gb`, `tb`

**Volume:**
- `ml`, `l` (liters), `gal` (gallons)

**Mass:**
- `g`, `kg` (kilograms), `lb`, `oz`

**Home Assistant:**
- `brightness` (0-255 ↔ 0-100%)
- `percent` (0-100)

### Try it

```yaml lab
entity: sensor.demo_temperature
processing:
  fahrenheit:
    type: convert_unit
    from: c
    to: f
```

### Examples

```yaml
# Temperature conversion
fahrenheit:
  type: convert_unit
  from: c
  to: f

# Power to kilowatts
kilowatts:
  type: convert_unit
  from: w
  to: kw

# Brightness to percentage
percent:
  type: convert_unit
  from: brightness
  to: percent
```

---

## `scale`

Map input range to output range with optional curve.

### Configuration

```yaml
processor_name:
  type: scale
  input_source: source_processor  # Optional
  input_range: [0, 100]
  output_range: [0, 255]
  curve: linear                   # linear, exponential, logarithmic, sigmoid
```

### Try it

```yaml lab
entity: sensor.demo_humidity
processing:
  normalized:
    type: scale
    input_range: [0, 100]
    output_range: [0, 1]
```

### Examples

```yaml
# Normalize 0-100 to 0-1
normalized:
  type: scale
  input_range: [0, 100]
  output_range: [0, 1]

# Temperature comfort index
comfort:
  type: scale
  input_source: fahrenheit
  input_range: [32, 95]
  output_range: [0, 100]

# RGB brightness
rgb:
  type: scale
  input_range: [0, 100]
  output_range: [0, 255]
  curve: exponential  # More natural brightness perception
```

---

## `smooth`

Apply smoothing algorithms to reduce noise.

### Configuration

```yaml
processor_name:
  type: smooth
  input_source: source_processor  # Optional
  method: exponential             # exponential, moving_average, gaussian
  window: 10                      # moving_average and gaussian: samples (default 10)
  alpha: 0.3                      # For exponential (0-1, lower = more smoothing)
```

### Methods

**Exponential:**
- Lightweight (single value state)
- Good for real-time displays
- `alpha`: 0.1 (heavy) to 0.9 (light smoothing)

**Moving Average:**
- Accurate averaging
- Requires buffer of `window` samples
- Good for historical analysis

**Gaussian:**
- Weighted average with bell curve
- Smoothest result
- Computationally heavier

### Try it

```yaml lab
# A spiky power sensor: compare the three methods
entity: sensor.demo_power
processing:
  exponential:
    type: smooth
    method: exponential
    alpha: 0.2
  moving_average:
    type: smooth
    method: moving_average
    window: 6
  gaussian:
    type: smooth
    method: gaussian
    window: 6
```

### Examples

```yaml
# Light exponential smoothing
smoothed:
  type: smooth
  method: exponential
  alpha: 0.3

# 10-sample moving average
moving_avg:
  type: smooth
  input_source: converted
  method: moving_average
  window: 10

# Smooth temperature readings
smooth_temp:
  type: smooth
  input_source: fahrenheit
  method: gaussian
  window: 5
```

---

## `expression`

Evaluate custom JavaScript expressions.

### Configuration

```yaml
processor_name:
  type: expression
  input_source: source_processor  # Optional: single source
  sources:                        # Optional: multiple sources
    - processor1
    - processor2
  expression: "value * 2"    # JavaScript expression
```

### Context Variables

- `value`, `v` - Current value: the `input_source` processor's output, else the raw entity value
- `timestamp`, `t` - Time of the value (epoch ms)
- `sources[0], sources[1]...` - The outputs of the processors listed in `sources` (they always run first)
- `entity` - The entity's state object (`state`, `attributes`, `entity_id`, `last_changed`, `last_updated`)
- `buffer` - The data source's raw value buffer
- `Math`, plus the shortcuts `abs`, `min`, `max`, `round`, `floor`, `ceil`, `pow`, `sqrt`

The expression is a single JavaScript expression (it is evaluated as `return (expression)`), so use the conditional operator rather than `if` or `return` statements. An expression that throws returns no value for that sample.

### Try it

```yaml lab
# How far the temperature is from its 24 h mean
entity: sensor.demo_temperature
processing:
  daily:
    type: statistics
    window: 24h
    stats: [mean]
  deviation:
    type: expression
    sources: [daily]
    expression: "value - sources[0].mean"
```

### Examples

```yaml
# Simple calculation
doubled:
  type: expression
  expression: "value * 2"

# Temperature-humidity comfort formula
comfort:
  type: expression
  sources:
    - temperature
    - humidity
  expression: "sources[0] - ((100 - sources[1]) * 0.5)"

# Conditional logic
status:
  type: expression
  input_source: temperature
  expression: "value > 25 ? 'hot' : 'cold'"

# Complex formula
feels_like:
  type: expression
  sources:
    - temp_f
    - humidity
    - wind_speed
  expression: "sources[0] + 0.33 * sources[1] - 0.7 * sources[2] - 4.0"
```

---

## `statistics`

Calculate statistical measures over a time window.

### Configuration

```yaml
processor_name:
  type: statistics
  input_source: source_processor  # Optional
  window: 24h                     # Time window or 'session'
  stats:                  # Array of statistics to calculate
    - min
    - max
    - mean
```

### Available Statistics

- `min` - Minimum value
- `max` - Maximum value
- `mean` - Average
- `median` - Middle value
- `std_dev` - Standard deviation
- `q1` - 25th percentile
- `q3` - 75th percentile
- `range` - max - min
- `count` - Number of samples
- `sum` - Sum of the values

`avg` and `stddev` are accepted as aliases of `mean` and `std_dev`. Defaults: `window: session`, `stats: [min, max, mean]`. A time window covers this processor's own recent inputs, up to the data source's buffer size (`window_seconds` x 10 points, at least 60; 600 by default).

### Output

Returns an object with the requested stats, plus `oldest` and `newest` (timestamps of the first and last value in the window) and `window`:
```javascript
{
  min: 18.5,
  max: 24.3,
  mean: 21.2,
  median: 21.0,
  count: 144,
  oldest: 1760000000000,
  newest: 1760086400000,
  window: '24h'
}
```

With `max_points: N` it returns the last N of these results as a time series (each with a `t` timestamp) instead.

### Try it

```yaml lab
entity: sensor.demo_outdoor_temperature
processing:
  last_hour:
    type: statistics
    window: 1h
    stats: [min, max, mean]
```

### Examples

```yaml
# Daily temperature statistics
daily_stats:
  type: statistics
  input_source: fahrenheit
  window: 24h
  stats: [min, max, mean]

# Session-wide stats
session_stats:
  type: statistics
  window: session
  stats: [min, max, range]

# Full statistical analysis
complete_stats:
  type: statistics
  input_source: sensor_value
  window: 1h
  stats: [min, max, mean, median, std_dev, q1, q3]
```

**Template Access:**
```yaml
overlays:
  - content: "Min: {temp.daily_stats.min:.1f}°F"
  - content: "Max: {temp.daily_stats.max:.1f}°F"
  - content: "Avg: {temp.daily_stats.mean:.1f}°F"
```

## `trend`

Detect trend direction (increasing, decreasing, stable).

### Configuration

```yaml
processor_name:
  type: trend
  input_source: source_processor  # Optional
  samples: 5                      # Number of samples to analyze
  threshold: 0.01                 # Minimum change to detect trend
```

### Output

Returns string:
- `"increasing"` - Value trending up
- `"decreasing"` - Value trending down
- `"stable"` - No significant change

### Try it

```yaml lab
# trend outputs a word, so it shows in the table, not the chart
entity: sensor.demo_outdoor_temperature
processing:
  smoothed:
    type: smooth
    alpha: 0.3
  direction:
    type: trend
    input_source: smoothed
    samples: 6
    threshold: 0.02
```

### Examples

```yaml
# Temperature trend
temp_trend:
  type: trend
  input_source: celsius
  samples: 10
  threshold: 0.1

# Battery trend
battery_trend:
  type: trend
  input_source: battery_percent
  samples: 5
  threshold: 1
```

**Template Usage:**
```yaml
overlays:
  - content: "Trend: {temp.temp_trend}"  # "increasing"
  - content: |
      {% if temp.temp_trend == 'increasing' %}↗{% endif %}
```

## `duration`

Track time spent in a condition.

### Configuration

```yaml
processor_name:
  type: duration
  input_source: source_processor  # Optional
  condition: "> 20"               # Condition expression
  reset_on: "< 15"                # Optional: reset condition
```

### Output

Returns object:
```javascript
{
  duration_ms: 3600000,           // Milliseconds
  duration_human: "1h 0m",        // Human-readable
  in_condition: true              // Whether the condition holds now
}
```

Conditions compare numbers (`>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `==`, `!=`). On/off entities arrive as `1`/`0` (other text states need `enum_mapping` on the data source), so test them with `== 1`.

### Try it

```yaml lab
# Minutes spent above 21.5 °C (resets each time it drops below)
entity: sensor.demo_temperature
processing:
  warm:
    type: duration
    condition: "> 21.5"
```

### Examples

```yaml
# Time above threshold
high_temp_duration:
  type: duration
  input_source: celsius
  condition: "> 25"
  reset_on: "< 20"

# Motion detection duration (binary_sensor: on = 1)
motion_duration:
  type: duration
  condition: "== 1"

# Door open duration (binary_sensor: open = on = 1)
door_open_time:
  type: duration
  condition: "== 1"
```

**Template Access:**
```yaml
overlays:
  - content: "High temp for: {temp.high_temp_duration.duration_human}"
```

---

## `threshold`

Convert value to binary based on threshold.

### Configuration

```yaml
processor_name:
  type: threshold
  input_source: source_processor  # Optional
  threshold: 20
  above: 1                        # Value when above threshold
  below: 0                        # Value when below threshold
  hysteresis: 2                   # Optional: prevent flapping
```

### Hysteresis

Prevents rapid switching near the threshold. `hysteresis` is the width of a dead band centred on the threshold:
- When rising: switches to `above` at `threshold + hysteresis / 2`
- When falling: switches to `below` at `threshold - hysteresis / 2`

The first value picks the starting state against `threshold` itself.

### Try it

```yaml lab
# 1 when warm, 0 when not; the 1 °C band stops flapping around 21.5
entity: sensor.demo_temperature
processing:
  warm:
    type: threshold
    threshold: 21.5
    hysteresis: 1
```

### Examples

```yaml
# Simple binary
is_hot:
  type: threshold
  input_source: celsius
  threshold: 25
  above: 1
  below: 0

# With hysteresis (prevents flapping at 25°C)
comfort_alert:
  type: threshold
  input_source: temperature
  threshold: 25
  above: 1
  below: 0
  hysteresis: 2  # Switches at 26°C rising, 24°C falling

# Custom values
temp_level:
  type: threshold
  input_source: fahrenheit
  threshold: 75
  above: "hot"
  below: "comfortable"
```

## `round`

Round to specified precision.

### Configuration

```yaml
processor_name:
  type: round
  input_source: source_processor  # Optional
  precision: 1                    # Decimal places
  method: round                   # round, floor, ceil
```

### Methods

- `round` - Standard rounding (0.5 → 1)
- `floor` - Always round down (0.9 → 0)
- `ceil` - Always round up (0.1 → 1)

### Try it

```yaml lab
    type: round
    precision: 0
    method: floor
```

```yaml
  type: round
  precision: 1

# No decimals

  type: round
  input_source: temperature
  precision: 0

# Always round down

  type: round
  input_source: value
  precision: 0
  method: floor

# Round to nearest 5

  type: expression
  expression: "Math.round(value / 5) * 5"
```


## Chaining Processors

Processors can depend on each other using `input_source` (and an expression's `sources`):

```yaml lab
data_sources:
  temp:
    entity: sensor.temperature
    processing:
      # 1. Convert to Fahrenheit (no dependencies)
      fahrenheit:
        type: convert_unit
        from: c
        to: f

      # 2. Smooth (depends on fahrenheit)
      smoothed:
        type: smooth
        input_source: fahrenheit
        method: exponential
        alpha: 0.3

      # 3. Round (depends on smoothed)
      rounded:
        type: round
        input_source: smoothed
        precision: 1

      # 4. Statistics (depends on smoothed, parallel with rounded)
      stats:
        type: statistics
        input_source: smoothed
        window: 24h
        stats: [min, max, mean]
```

**Execution Order:**
1. `fahrenheit` (no dependencies)
2. `smoothed` (depends on `fahrenheit`)
3. `rounded` and `stats` (both depend on `smoothed`)

Each value runs through the whole chain in that order before the next value arrives.

---

## Performance Notes

**Lightweight Processors:**
- `convert_unit`, `scale`, `round`, `clamp`, `threshold`, `delta`
- Single-pass calculations, minimal memory

**Medium Weight:**
- `smooth` (exponential)
- `expression` (simple formulas)
- `rate`, `trend`

**Heavier Processors:**
- `smooth` (moving average, gaussian)
- `statistics` (requires window buffer)
- `duration`
- `expression` (complex formulas)

**Best Practices:**
1. Only create processors you actually use
2. Use `update_interval` to throttle high-frequency sources
3. Prefer exponential smoothing over moving average for displays
4. Limit statistics windows to what you need
5. Avoid deeply nested processor chains (>5 levels)

---

<!-- https://lcards.unimatrix01.ca/dev/core/effects/background-animations/binding-and-animation.html -->

# Binding and Animation

A background can react to Home Assistant in two ways: a `config` value can follow an entity, and an animation can change the background when a trigger fires or a rule matches. The keys of one entry are on the [Background Animations](/core/effects/background-animations#effect-options) page.

## Entity binding

**Any value in an effect's `config` can follow an entity: give it a `map_range` or a template instead of a fixed value.** Use it for a grid that scrolls faster as power rises, or a level that fills with a tank sensor.

- [`map_range`](#map-range) maps a number from the entity onto the key's range, with no template to write. [Templates](#templates) are for anything else.
- The [animatable keys](#animatable-keys) glide to the new value over the entry's `transition` (500 ms unless you set it); other keys snap or stay fixed, see [Which keys follow an entity](#which-keys-follow-an-entity).
- The card editor shows this as a tip; you write the binding in the card's YAML.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: outline
entity: input_number.lcards_test_value
text:
  name:
    content: SCAN RATE
    show: true
grid_options:
  rows: 3
background_animation:
  # scroll speed follows the value, gliding over 1.5 s
  - preset: grid
    transition: 1500
    config:
      color: alpha(var(--lcars-orange), 0.4)
      scroll_speed_x:
        map_range:
          input: [0, 100]
          output: [0, 120]
```

::: details More about entity binding
- **Also in `shape_texture`:** a button's or elbow's [shape texture](/cards/button/textures#shape-texture) reads `map_range` and template strings in its `config` the same way, without the glide.
- **The first value snaps:** the value the card loads with is applied at once; only later changes glide. `transition: 0` and reduced motion always snap.
- **When it updates:** bound values are worked out again on every Home Assistant update.
:::

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `config.<key>` | value / object / string | - | A fixed value, a [`map_range`](#map-range) object, or a [template](#templates) |
| `transition` | number | `500` | Milliseconds a bound animatable key takes to glide to a new value; `0` snaps |

### map_range

**`map_range` reads a number from an entity and maps it from the `input` range onto the `output` range.** `brightness` 0 to 255 onto a scroll speed of -200 to 200, say.

- Without `attribute` it reads the entity's state; the value must be a number.
- Without `entity` it reads the card's own `entity`. On the MSD and astrometrics cards, which have no card entity, set it.
- A value outside `input` is held at the ends of `output` unless `clamp: false`.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: outline
entity: light.bridge
text:
  name:
    content: PLASMA FLOW
    show: true
grid_options:
  rows: 3
background_animation:
  - preset: plasma
    config:
      # the light's brightness sets how fast the plasma drifts
      scroll_speed_x:
        map_range:
          attribute: brightness
          input: [0, 255]
          output: [-200, 200]
      scroll_speed_y:
        map_range:
          attribute: brightness
          input: [0, 255]
          output: [5, 60]
```

::: details More about map_range
- **Colours too:** with two colours as `output`, a colour key is blended between them, transparency too. Each can be any colour LCARdS accepts (a hex of any length, a named colour, `rgb()` or `hsl()`, a CSS variable, a `theme:` token or a computed colour such as `alpha()`); colours always hold at the ends of `output`.
- **A value that isn't a number:** the key keeps its current value and a warning is logged in the browser console.
- **The older name:** `entity_id` still works in place of `entity`, as in earlier versions.
:::

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `map_range.entity` | string | the card's `entity` | The entity to read |
| `map_range.attribute` | string | the state | The attribute to read instead of the state |
| `map_range.input` | `[min, max]` | required | The range of the entity's value |
| `map_range.output` | `[min, max]` | required | The range of the key's value: two numbers or two colours |
| `map_range.clamp` | boolean | `true` | Hold the result inside `output` |

### Templates

**A template string works out the value in JavaScript (`[[[ ... ]]]`) or from tokens (`{entity.state}`).** The result is a number when it looks like one, otherwise a string such as a colour.

- In JavaScript, `entity` is the card's entity, and `hass`, `config` and `variables` are there too. Home Assistant (Jinja) templates are not evaluated in a background.
- The object form, `template` with `default`, always gives a number: `default` when the template's result isn't one.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: outline
entity: input_number.lcards_test_value
text:
  name:
    content: TANK
    show: true
grid_options:
  rows: 3
background_animation:
  - preset: level
    config:
      # the fill follows the value
      fill_pct: "[[[ return Number(entity.state) ]]]"
      # faster waves as it fills, 20 until the value is known
      wave_speed:
        template: "[[[ return 10 + Number(entity.state) / 2 ]]]"
        default: 20
```

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `config.<key>` | string | - | A `[[[ JavaScript ]]]` or `{token}` template |
| `config.<key>.template` | string | required | The template, in the object form |
| `config.<key>.default` | number | `0` | The value when the template's result isn't a number |

### Which keys follow an entity

**How a bound value is applied depends on the key: it glides, it snaps, or it can't change after the effect starts.**

- **Glides:** the [animatable keys](#animatable-keys) move to the new value over `transition`.
- **Snaps:** other keys of `level`, `fluid`, `plasma`, `flow`, `shimmer`, `scanlines`, `image` and `contour-field` change at once (the field is worked out again, the image reloads).
- **Fixed:** other keys of `grid`, `grid-diagonal`, `grid-hexagonal`, `starfield`, `nebula`, `cascade`, `solid`, `warp-starfield` and `holo-sphere` (a star `count`, a grid `pattern`) are set when the effect is created. A binding on one is logged once in the browser console and does nothing.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: outline
entity: input_number.lcards_test_value
text:
  name:
    content: STARS
    show: true
grid_options:
  rows: 3
background_animation:
  - preset: starfield
    config:
      count: 200 # fixed: set once
      # glides: an animatable key
      scroll_speed_x:
        map_range:
          input: [0, 100]
          output: [10, 200]
```

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `transition` | number | `500` | Glide time for the animatable keys, ms |

## Animating the background

**An animation can change the card's background effects instead of a part of the card: set `target: background`.** A trigger, a `while` condition or a rule (`apply.animations`) can then ramp a starfield to warp on red alert, or tint a grid.

- `effect` picks one entry by its place in the list (`0` is the first, the bottom layer, and disabled entries count); without it, every entry is animated.
- Use `preset: custom` and put the effect's keys in `params`, written like any anime.js property: `[from, to]`, a single end value, or keyframes. Only the [animatable keys](#animatable-keys) can move.
- Easing, `loop`, `alternate` and reduced motion work as for any [animation](/core/animations). Stopping a running animation puts the values back.

```yaml live controls
type: custom:lcards-button
preset: outline
entity: input_select.lcards_alert_mode
text:
  name:
    content: WARP
    show: true
grid_options:
  rows: 3
background_animation:
  - preset: starfield
    zoom:
      layers: 4
      duration: 12
    config:
      scroll_speed_x: 0
animations:
  # ramp the stars (and the zoom cycle) to 8x over 2 s when red alert starts
  - trigger: on_entity_change
    entity: input_select.lcards_alert_mode
    to_state: red_alert
    target: background
    effect: 0
    preset: custom
    params:
      speed: [1, 8]
      duration: 2000
      ease: inOutQuad
  # and back down when it ends
  - trigger: on_entity_change
    entity: input_select.lcards_alert_mode
    from_state: red_alert
    target: background
    effect: 0
    preset: custom
    params:
      speed: 1
      duration: 3000
      ease: outQuad
```

::: details More about animating the background
- **Through an alert:** the animation keeps running when an alert mode recolours the background; the effects are rebuilt with the new palette and pick up the animated values.
- **Without animations:** the same warp works with a binding. A template picks the speed and `transition` sets the glide:

  ```yaml
  background_animation:
    - preset: starfield
      transition: 2000
      config:
        speed: "[[[ return entity.state === 'red_alert' ? 8 : 1 ]]]"
  ```
- **A key that can't move:** naming one in `params` is logged once in the browser console.
:::

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `target` | string | - | `background`: animate the card's background effects |
| `effect` | number | every entry | The entry to animate, by its place in the list (`0` is the first) |
| `preset` | string | - | `custom`, with the effect's keys in `params` |
| `params` | object | - | The [animatable keys](#animatable-keys) to change, plus `duration`, `ease` and the other animation timing keys |

## Animatable keys

**These are the keys an animation can move and a binding can glide.** Every effect also takes `opacity` and the transform keys `x` and `y` (offset in px), `rotate` (degrees) and `scale` (about the centre); every effect that moves takes `speed`. Colour keys accept every LCARdS colour form.

- Other keys are left out on purpose: changing them means rebuilding the effect (a new star layout, a field worked out again), too slow to do every frame.
- The WebGL versions of the noise presets have nothing to rebuild, so their noise keys are animatable there; under `renderer: canvas` or without WebGL they have the Canvas2D list.

| Preset | Keys |
|---|---|
| `grid`, `grid-diagonal`, `grid-hexagonal` | `scroll_speed_x`, `scroll_speed_y`, `line_spacing`, `line_width`, `line_width_minor`, `line_width_major`, `color`, `color_major`, `fill_color` (those the preset takes); `grid` also `spoke_count`, `polar_x`, `polar_y`; on WebGL also `camera_tilt`, `camera_yaw`, `camera_roll`, `camera_distance`, `fov`, `scan_color`, `surface_size`, `surface_length`, `back_opacity`, `surface_rotate_x`, `surface_rotate_y`, `surface_rotate_z`, `well_throat`, `well_morph`, `well_ripple`, `well_ripple_waves`, `well_ripple_speed` |
| `starfield` | `scroll_speed_x`, `scroll_speed_y`, `color` (one colour for every star) |
| `nebula` | `scroll_speed_x`, `scroll_speed_y`, `turbulence` |
| `contour-field` | `scroll_speed_x`, `scroll_speed_y`; on WebGL also `noise_scale`, `num_bands`, `fill_level` |
| `cascade` | (the common keys) |
| `level` | `fill_pct`, `wave_height`, `wave_speed`, `wave2_height`, `wave2_speed`, `slosh_amount` |
| `fluid` | `scroll_speed_x`, `scroll_speed_y`; on WebGL also `base_frequency`, `color` |
| `plasma` | `scroll_speed_x`, `scroll_speed_y`; on WebGL also `base_frequency`, `color_a`, `color_b` |
| `flow` | `scroll_speed_x`, `scroll_speed_y`, `wave_scale` |
| `scanlines` | `scroll_speed_x`, `scroll_speed_y`, `line_spacing`, `line_width` |
| `shimmer` | `highlight_width`, `angle` |
| `image` | `opacity` and the transform keys (no `speed`) |
| `solid` | `opacity`, `color` and the transform keys (no `speed`) |
| `warp-starfield` | `streak`, `camera_tilt`, `camera_yaw`, `camera_roll`, `fov`, `color` |
| `holo-sphere` | `rotate_speed`, `tilt`, `size`, `position_x`, `position_y`, `back_opacity`, `line_width`, `color`, `scan_color` |
